title: The Copper Tap and the Unsigned Book: Locke from Wrington to High Laver
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Wrington, the baptism at All Saints
stops.date_confidence: attested; born and baptized the same day. Coordinates corrected: all three research lenses placed Wrington 2.5 to 6 km east of the village, out toward Butcombe. Standardised on the Church of All Saints, OS grid ST4691664026.
stops.campa: In the Somerset village of Wrington, under the northern edge of the Mendips, a country attorney's wife bears a son, and the child is carried to the parish church of All Saints the same day and baptized John. The father holds a small estate and a clerkship to the county justices. The mother is a tanner's daughter, older than her husband. The house is Puritan: plain worship, scripture read aloud, the magistrate obeyed only so far as conscience will allow. Two centuries later the village sets his bust beside the door of this church.
sources: H. R. Fox Bourne, The Life of John Locke (1876)
suggested_refs: The Church of All Saints, Wrington, and its baptismal register for August 1632

stops.name: Pensford, the lawyer's house south of Bristol
stops.date_confidence: contested between lenses and not resolved. The geography lens dates the move to 1632, 'shortly after Locke's birth', following Wikipedia. The chronology lens dates it to 1642, bundling it with the father's Parliamentary service. Ten years apart. Dated here as a reading of 'shortly after'; the 1642 alternative stands unrefuted.
stops.campa: The family removes about seven miles south of Bristol to Pensford, where the father practises law and keeps the small properties that will one day pass, diminished, to his elder son. When the war comes in 1642 the attorney rides out as a captain of horse for Parliament, in the regiment of Alexander Popham, a Somerset member. The boy grows up in a household where the fighting is a matter of muster rolls and quartering, in a county that changes hands more than once. His father's colonel will shortly buy him a place at the best school in England.
suggested_refs: Pensford, Somerset, and the Parliamentary muster rolls of the western association

stops.name: Belluton, the farmhouse of the boyhood
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No primary document fixes the house; the identification descends through county histories and local telling, and the coordinates are approximate. The date is a placeholder for the boyhood years, not an event.
stops.campa: A Tudor farmhouse at Belluton, a hamlet on the ridge above Pensford, is remembered as the house of his childhood. No deed fixes it. The identification comes down through county histories and local telling, and the building survives only in fragments worked into later walls. What the tradition preserves is the scale of the thing: a small freehold, a lawyer's income, a few tenants, a horizon of Somerset coal pits and grazing land. The philosopher of property begins among a modest quantity of it, and inherits less than his father held.
sources: local and antiquarian tradition, relayed via county histories and Age-of-the-Sage
suggested_refs: The surviving fragments of the Belluton farmhouse near Pensford

stops.name: Westminster School, the birch of Richard Busby
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: At fifteen the boy is entered at Westminster School under Richard Busby, whose Latin is famous and whose birch is more famous still. The school stands inside the Abbey precinct, a few hundred yards from Whitehall, and the place there comes through Alexander Popham, his father's colonel in the Parliamentary horse and now a member of the Commons. Locke construes Greek and Hebrew under a discipline of flogging. Forty-six years later he publishes a book on education arguing that children are not to be beaten into learning.
suggested_refs: Westminster School, Dean's Yard, under Richard Busby's headmastership

stops.name: Christ Church, admitted at twenty
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1652; day not recorded.
stops.campa: He is admitted to Christ Church, Oxford, and takes up a studentship that will hold him, with interruptions, for thirty-two years. The curriculum is scholastic: disputation, Aristotle, the syllogism worked over ground already worked to dust. He finds it tedious and says so. What holds him instead is the experimental work going on in the town, the chemistry and the anatomy and the physicians who practise it. He remains based here through his degrees, his lectureships, and his patron's rise, and leaves only when a king has his name struck off the roll.
suggested_refs: The studentship rolls of Christ Church, Oxford, 1652-1684

stops.name: Christ Church, the two degrees
stops.date_confidence: attested: BA February 1656, MA June 1658. The firmest pair of dates in the Oxford years; both lenses agree.
stops.campa: Bachelor of Arts in February 1656, Master of Arts in June 1658, and with the master's degree the senior studentship at Christ Church, a place he can hold as long as he satisfies its conditions. He is twenty-five and settled in an institution he does not admire. What he takes from Oxford is not its philosophy but its medicine and its instruments: dissection, chemistry, the recording of cases at the bedside. He begins the commonplace books, everything read entered under headings of his own devising, and keeps them for the next twenty years.
suggested_refs: Locke's commonplace books and their indexing method, Lovelace Collection, Bodleian Library

stops.name: Christ Church, the lectureships
stops.date_confidence: the posts are attested, the years are contested. SEP gives Lecturer in Greek December 1660 and Lecturer in Rhetoric 1663; the geography lens gives Rhetoric 1662; the standard chronologies of Cranston and Woolhouse put Censor of Moral Philosophy in 1664 where the geography lens puts it in 1663. Not adjudicated.
stops.campa: Lecturer in Greek from December 1660, Lecturer in Rhetoric after that, then Censor of Moral Philosophy: the ordinary ladder of a college officer, climbed as the monarchy comes back. The chronologies disagree about the rungs. One puts Rhetoric in 1662 and the censorship in 1663; another gives Rhetoric 1663 and the censorship 1664. Locke is thirty-one, unpublished, and known in Oxford as a competent tutor with an unusual interest in medicine. Nothing he has written is going to be printed for another twenty-six years.
suggested_refs: The Christ Church officer lists for 1660-1664, and the Cranston and Woolhouse chronologies that disagree over them

stops.name: Kleve, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested: November 1665 to February 1666; the day of arrival is not recorded.
stops.campa: He leaves England for the first time at thirty-three, secretary to Sir Walter Vane on a mission to the Elector of Brandenburg, who keeps his court at the Schwanenburg above Kleve. The embassy is to buy Brandenburg out of the Dutch war and it fails. What does not fail is what he sees in the town: Lutherans, Calvinists, and Catholics keeping separate worship inside one small polity without cutting each other's throats. He writes home about it. The Letter Concerning Toleration is twenty years off.
suggested_refs: The Schwanenburg at Kleve, seat of the Elector of Brandenburg's court in 1665

stops.name: Christ Church, the patient from London
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the season is not fixed by the sources.
stops.campa: Anthony Ashley Cooper comes up to Oxford to take the medicinal waters at Astrop in Northamptonshire and wants a physician's opinion of them. Locke is asked to supply it, and the two men talk. Ashley is a politician with a genius for faction and a diseased liver, and he asks this Christ Church student to come into his household. Locke has no medical degree and no political opinions on record. Inside a year he has left Oxford for Ashley's London house on the Strand.
suggested_refs: The mineral spring at Astrop, Northamptonshire, and Ashley Cooper's 1666 course of the waters

segments.name: Exeter House: Physician to a Faction

stops.name: Exeter House, the copper tap
stops.date_confidence: attested: residency from May 1667, operation May 1668. The house was demolished; the coordinates are approximated from period maps of Exeter Street and are a reconstruction.
stops.campa: He moves into Exeter House on the Strand as Ashley's physician, tutor to his son, and secretary, a household post that is also an apprenticeship in government. In May 1668 he oversees the operation that makes his name inside that house: an abscess of the liver drained through an incision, the wound kept open afterward by a copper tap his patron carries in his side for the rest of his life. Ashley survives another twenty-five years. Tory pamphleteers will call him Tapski, for the pipe and for the elective Polish throne they accuse him of wanting.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury'
suggested_refs: The site of Exeter House on the Strand, and the Tory 'Tapski' pamphlets of the Exclusion years

stops.name: Arundel House, elected Fellow of the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1668; the venue is corrected. The research pool placed the election at Gresham College, but the Society had quit Gresham after the Great Fire of 1666 and did not return until 1673, so the 1668 election falls in the Arundel House period. Pin inherited byte-identical from newton.journey.json, which flags the same venue correction.
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects him Fellow. It is meeting at Arundel House on the Strand in these years, the Great Fire having driven it out of Gresham College, and it will not go back until 1673. Among the Fellows are Robert Boyle, whose air-pump work Locke has followed since Oxford, and Thomas Sydenham, with whom he keeps clinical notebooks at the bedsides of London patients. Isaac Newton is twenty-six that year, unknown outside Cambridge, and not yet of the company. The two of them will correspond for the rest of Locke's life.
suggested_refs: Arundel House on the Strand, meeting place of the Royal Society 1666-1673

stops.name: Exeter House, the Carolina papers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1669 for the Carolina drafting and to October 1673 for the Council of Trade appointment; the month of the Carolina work is not fixed.
stops.campa: Ashley is one of the Lords Proprietors of a colony on the American coast, and Locke, as his secretary, is directed to help draft the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina. In October 1673 he is made Secretary to the Council of Trade and Plantations, and the colonial administration of England begins crossing his desk: plantations, shipping, the terms on which men labour overseas. The philosopher of consent is also a clerk of empire, in the same hand and the same decade.
stops.quote: Thus in the beginning all the world was America, and more so than that is now.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), Chapter V, Section 49; Project Gutenberg ebook 7370
suggested_refs: The Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina (1669) and the papers of the Council of Trade and Plantations

stops.name: Exeter House, the evening the Essay began
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1671 by Locke's own account in the Epistle to the Reader; no month is given there.
stops.campa: Five or six friends meet in his chamber to argue a question of morality and revealed religion, and get nowhere at all. The difficulties are not in the subject, Locke decides, but in the instrument: they have been reasoning without first asking what reason can reach. He proposes they examine their own understandings before going further, writes some hasty thoughts on a sheet of paper that night, and does not finish the work for nineteen years. He tells the story himself in the Epistle to the Reader, and dates the whole Essay from that evening.
stops.quote: to inquire into the original, certainty, and extent of HUMAN KNOWLEDGE, together with the grounds and degrees of BELIEF, OPINION, and ASSENT
stops.quote_source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book I, Chapter I, Section 2; Project Gutenberg ebook 10615
sources: Locke, Epistle to the Reader, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
suggested_refs: Drafts A and B of the Essay (1671), the earliest surviving states of the text

stops.name: Christ Church, Bachelor of Medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1675; day not recorded.
stops.campa: Oxford gives him the degree of Bachelor of Medicine in February, twenty-three years after he first came up and long after he began practising. He is forty-two, asthmatic, and living in a London whose coal smoke his lungs will not take. Shaftesbury is out of office and into opposition, and the household that has employed Locke for eight years has become a liability to belong to. In November he takes ship for France without his commonplace books, and stays away three and a half years.
suggested_refs: The Oxford medical faculty registers for February 1675

stops.name: Calais, landing without the books
stops.date_confidence: attested; the source gives the crossing as 12/24 November 1675, Old Style over New Style. English and continental dates in this journey are ten days apart and are not normalised.
stops.campa: He crosses to Calais in November and lands without the commonplace books that have organised his reading since Oxford. In their place he keeps a journal: a running record by date, distances in leagues, prices, weather, the state of the vines, what a physician in a strange town says about a case. A man who has spent twenty years filing knowledge under headings begins instead to record it in the order it arrives at him. He does this for three and a half years and fills volumes with it.
sources: 'John Locke's Note-taking in France, 1675-1679', Studi Lockiani
suggested_refs: Locke's French journals, 1675-1679, Lovelace Collection, Bodleian Library

stops.name: Paris, the passage south
stops.date_confidence: attested that he passed through Paris southbound in 1675-1676 and returned repeatedly; no single dated visit is pinned. Coordinates: the canonical atlas Paris pin, inherited byte-identical, in preference to the research lens value of 48.853, 2.3499.
stops.campa: Paris, on the way south and repeatedly afterward. He moves among English residents, physicians, and virtuosi, sees the collections and the hospitals, notes what the French do differently in anatomy and in gardening. The journals record the city the way a working traveller records one, by lodging, price, and letter of introduction, not by monument. He is forty-three, he has a bad chest, he has published nothing, and nobody in Paris has heard of him.
sources: John Lough (ed.), Locke's Travels in France, 1675-1679 (Cambridge, 1953), via secondary report
suggested_refs: Lough's edition of the French journals, which prints the Paris entries in full

stops.name: Montpellier, fifteen months of southern air
stops.date_confidence: attested to roughly fifteen months across 1676-1677; the month of arrival is not fixed by the reachable sources.
stops.campa: He settles at Montpellier for roughly fifteen months, drawn by the oldest medical faculty in France and by a town full of English residents and Huguenots. He botanises, attends the faculty, and watches Protestant worship conducted under a monarchy that is closing it down. His notebooks fill with observation of how a religious minority actually lives beside a majority, which is a different question from how it ought to. Montpellier's air is prescribed to consumptives. Locke breathes it for a year and a quarter and gets better.
suggested_refs: The medical faculty of Montpellier and its English and Huguenot community in the 1670s

stops.name: Gigean, three leagues out
stops.date_confidence: the route is attested; the 27 February 1677 journal date could not be verified without Lough's printed edition, which was not reachable. Coordinates corrected: the pool value of 43.5486, 3.8232 lands about 10 km northeast of the village.
stops.campa: The journal for the twenty-seventh of February records the road out of Montpellier: three leagues to Gigean, a village under the Gardiole ridge on the way to Pezenas. The entry survives because he logs the distance at every stop, in leagues, as a matter of habit. Nothing happens at Gigean. It is a place he passes through and writes down, and because he wrote it down it is fixed in the record of his life more precisely than the year his own family moved house.
sources: Locke's journal, quoted in secondary discussion of Lough's edition
suggested_refs: The Montpellier to Pezenas road under the Gardiole ridge, as logged in leagues

stops.name: Pezenas, five leagues further the same day
stops.date_confidence: same entry, same caveat: the route is geographically sound and attested in secondary report of Lough; the journal date is unverified at first hand.
stops.campa: Five leagues on from Gigean the same day, Pezenas: a small Languedoc town of cloth and cattle fairs, one of the seats of the provincial estates. Locke is making a circuit out of Montpellier, gathering what a travelling physician gathers, and enters the town in his book with its distance and no adjectives. These southern pages were printed in full only in 1953, two hundred and seventy-six years after the day they record. The journals themselves sit in the Bodleian, in the Lovelace collection, and Locke published no line of them in his life.
sources: Locke's journal, quoted in secondary discussion of Lough's edition
suggested_refs: John Lough (ed.), Locke's Travels in France, 1675-1679 (Cambridge, 1953)

stops.name: Dover, the return that the journals do not name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia gives only 'returned to England' in 1679, April or May. The port is inferred from the standard Calais packet route and is not separately attested. The research pool's description of a 'second tour' beginning in 1679 is rejected: the stay was one continuous absence, November 1675 to spring 1679.
stops.campa: He comes back in the spring of 1679, three and a half years gone, across the Channel by the packet that has always run to Dover. Which port receives him the journals do not say; the crossing from Calais lands there, and the reconstruction is no stronger than that. England is in the middle of the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis. Shaftesbury is back near the centre of power and about to be flung out of it again. Locke returns to a household that is preparing, in a room he is not yet in, to justify resistance to a king.
sources: inference from the standard Calais-Dover packet route
suggested_refs: The Calais-Dover packet service and its 1679 sailings

segments.name: The Exclusion Crisis and the Flight

stops.name: Christ Church, the watched rooms
stops.date_confidence: the surveillance is attested across 1680-1683. The composition date of the Two Treatises is contested: the research pool offered 1682, but Laslett's dating, followed by Wikipedia and SEP, places the bulk of the writing in 1679-1681, with SEP giving 1681 and revisions after the 1683 flight. The 1682 figure falls outside the accepted window and is not used.
stops.campa: He divides his time between Oxford and London while Shaftesbury drives the Exclusion Bills at the King's brother. Royal agents watch him at Christ Church and report his movements, his visitors, and his silences. They suspect him of writing the anti-court tracts circulating in the town, and they are right about the man if not about the tract. In these years, by the accepted dating, he writes the Two Treatises of Government: not a justification composed after a revolution, but an argument for resistance written while resistance is still a hanging matter.
stops.quote: The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it, which obliges every one: and reason...teaches all mankind...that being all equal and independent, no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), Chapter II, Section 6; Project Gutenberg ebook 7370
suggested_refs: Peter Laslett's critical edition of the Two Treatises and its redating of the composition to 1679-1681

stops.name: London, Damaris Cudworth
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is dated 1682 by the biographical tradition; the character of the attachment is tradition only, with no primary correspondence quoted in any reachable source. The pool's phrase 'decades before settling permanently in her household' is corrected: met 1682, moved to Oates 1691, nine years.
stops.campa: He meets Damaris Cudworth, a philosopher in her own right and much the younger of the two. The biographical tradition, which quotes no correspondence to prove it, holds that the attachment between them was close and possibly more than that. She marries Sir Francis Masham. Locke never marries anyone at all. Nine years after this meeting he moves into the Mashams' Essex house as a permanent guest, stays for the last thirteen years of his life, and she is beside him at the end of it, reading aloud.
suggested_refs: The philosophical writings of Damaris Cudworth, Lady Masham

stops.name: Amsterdam, out of England in September
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1683; the day of sailing is not recorded. Coordinates: the canonical atlas Amsterdam pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: The Rye House Plot against Charles II and his brother is discovered, and the government moves on the Whigs of Shaftesbury's circle, arresting the ones it can reach and hanging some of them. In September Locke takes ship for the Dutch Republic, fifty-one years old, without waiting to learn whether any evidence against him exists. He is out of England five years and five months. Both of the books he will be known for are finished in that exile, and the letter on toleration is written there from nothing.
suggested_refs: The Rye House Plot depositions and the warrants issued against Shaftesbury's associates

stops.name: Leiden, the year under another man's name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to sequence. Sources agree that he moved among Amsterdam, Leiden, and Utrecht between September 1684 and May 1685, including six weeks of continuous travel in August-September 1684, but they do not fix the order or the addresses. The alias rests on two amateur-scholarly web sources with no archival citation reached.
stops.campa: Between September 1684 and the following May he moves repeatedly among Amsterdam, Leiden, and Utrecht, six weeks of it in one unbroken stretch of travel, living under the name Dr. van Linden. After the Monmouth rebellion the English government asks the Dutch to hand over a list of exiles and his name is on it. The sources agree on the set of cities and not on the order of them; the addresses are not fixed by the surviving letters. A philosopher of personal identity spends a year answering to another man's name.
suggested_refs: The English extradition list of 1685 and the Dutch response to it

stops.name: Christ Church, struck from the roll
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1684 by SEP; the chronology lens gives only the year.
stops.campa: Charles II writes to Christ Church, and the college removes John Locke from its list of students. The studentship he has held for twenty-six years, his address, his standing, and his Oxford income all end by royal letter, without charge and without hearing, while he is out of the country. He is fifty-two. The college will not have him back in his lifetime. Three centuries later its cathedral floor carries an engraved memorial to him, which notes that he came up from Westminster.
suggested_refs: The royal letter of November 1684 to the Dean and Chapter of Christ Church

stops.name: Amsterdam, the letter written in Latin
stops.date_confidence: the composition is placed in Amsterdam, winter 1685-86. The research pool's geography lens placed the writing at Rotterdam in 1686-1689, which contradicts its own chronology lens; the Rotterdam claim is not used and is recorded as the discarded alternative.
stops.campa: In the winter after Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes, with Huguenot refugees arriving in the Dutch cities by the thousand, Locke writes a letter in Latin to his friend Philipp van Limborch on the limits of the magistrate. The argument is that the care of souls cannot belong to the civil power, because belief cannot be compelled and a forced profession saves nobody. His own name is on the extradition list England has sent the Dutch that year. It is printed four years later and he does not put his name to it.
stops.quote: I esteem that toleration to be the chief characteristic mark of the true Church.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689, trans. William Popple from the Latin Epistola de Tolerantia), opening; Wikisource text
suggested_refs: The Epistola de Tolerantia in its Latin state, addressed to Philipp van Limborch

stops.name: Delft, at Leeuwenhoek's bench
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the visit is precisely dated in Locke's own journal. The best-fixed date of the Dutch years.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of June he goes to the Hippolytusbuurt in Delft, to the house of a draper who grinds lenses better than anyone alive, and looks through them. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek shows him red blood cells, a section of human tooth, and the spermatozoa of a dog: animals moving in a drop of fluid that no eye has ever seen unaided. Locke's journal fixes the day exactly. He is writing, in these same months, that every idea comes from sensation and reflection, and he has just watched the boundary of sensation move.
sources: lensonleeuwenhoek.net, 'Visited by John Locke', quoting Locke's journal
suggested_refs: Leeuwenhoek's house and laboratory on the Hippolytusbuurt, Delft

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Essay finished among the Remonstrants
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1686 for the completion of the Essay and for the Limborch association; no month given.
stops.campa: In Amsterdam he lives among the Remonstrants, the Dutch Arminians who hold that a church is a voluntary society and that salvation is not decreed in advance. Philipp van Limborch is their professor of theology and becomes his closest friend. Here Locke finishes the Essay Concerning Human Understanding, begun at Exeter House fifteen years earlier: four books arguing that the mind holds no principle it did not receive, that the child arrives with nothing written on it, and that the extent of what can be known is a great deal smaller than philosophy has assumed.
stops.quote: Mr. Locke has displayed the human soul in the same manner as an excellent anatomist explains the springs of the human body.
stops.quote_source: Voltaire, Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733), Letter XIII, 'On Mr. Locke'; Project Gutenberg ebook 2445
suggested_refs: The Remonstrant seminary at Amsterdam and Limborch's correspondence with Locke

stops.name: Rotterdam, the house called the Lantern
stops.date_confidence: the lodging with Benjamin Furly is attested for 1686-1689. The Erasmus University Library's further claim that Locke chaired a discussion society called De Lantaarn is not supported: Wikipedia's Furly article records the lodging and no club and no office, and De Lantaarn was the name of the house itself. Demoted to lodging and membership of Furly's circle.
stops.campa: His last Dutch years are spent largely at Rotterdam, in the house of the Quaker merchant Benjamin Furly, a house called De Lantaarn, the Lantern, holding one of the great private libraries of the Republic. Around Furly gathers a circle of dissenters, mystics, chemists, and political exiles out of half of Europe, arguing in three languages about scripture and the state. Locke lodges there, fifty-five years old, waiting on a change in England that most of the house expects and none of them can put a date to.
sources: Erasmus University Library, 'John Locke Collection' (claim of a chaired society not used)
suggested_refs: Benjamin Furly's library at De Lantaarn, Rotterdam, and its catalogue

segments.name: The Return, and the Books Nobody Signed

stops.name: Greenwich, ashore with the Princess
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12 February 1689 for the landing. The embarkation port of Hellevoetsluis is reconstructed from general histories of the 1689 fleet, not from any Locke-specific source. The pool's statement that he was fifty-seven is corrected: born August 1632, he was fifty-six that February.
stops.campa: He sails from the naval port of Hellevoetsluis in the fleet carrying Princess Mary to England, and comes ashore at Greenwich on the twelfth of February. William of Orange is already in London, and within the week the crown is offered to the two of them jointly. Locke is fifty-six, has been out of the country since 1683, and carries in his baggage a finished Essay and a manuscript on government written a decade earlier to justify resisting a king who has since been driven out without any help from it. Both go to the press this year.
sources: general histories of the Glorious Revolution fleet (embarkation port only)
suggested_refs: The February 1689 crossing of Princess Mary and the fleet from Hellevoetsluis

stops.name: Gouda, the Latin letter off van der Hoeve's press
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Latin Epistola was printed anonymously in the Netherlands, at Gouda, by Justus van der Hoeve; the research pool wrongly placed this publication in London, which was where Popple's English translation appeared. The month is not fixed. Coordinates are a town-centre lookup: this is the one pin in the file with no source-supplied value behind it.
stops.campa: The Epistola de Tolerantia is printed at Gouda by Justus van der Hoeve, with no author's name on it. Limborch has arranged the publication, and the Latin carries it across Europe without a translator. The same year William Popple, a Unitarian merchant, turns it into English and it appears in London, still anonymous, behind a preface of Popple's own calling for absolute liberty. Locke, back in England now, lets both editions stand unclaimed, and lets Popple's stronger preface stand in front of his own careful argument.
stops.quote: the care of souls is not committed to the civil magistrate, any more than to other men.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689, trans. William Popple); Wikisource text
sources: verifier correction on the place of the Latin imprint
suggested_refs: The Gouda imprint of the Epistola de Tolerantia, 1689, and Popple's English translation of the same year

stops.name: London, the two books of that December
stops.date_confidence: attested: both books are in the shops in late 1689, both title pages dated 1690. The Two Treatises is anonymous; the Essay carries his name.
stops.campa: In December the booksellers have both. An Essay Concerning Human Understanding goes out under his name, a folio the size of a doorstop. Two Treatises of Government goes out with no name at all, its title page dated 1690, its preface remarking of Sir Robert Filmer's defence of patriarchal kingship that a reader who reduced it to plain propositions would find what he found. Locke complains at once of errors in the printing and spends the rest of his life correcting the text. More than half the original manuscript is already lost.
stops.quote: there was never so much glib nonsense put together in well-sounding English.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, Preface to Two Treatises of Government (1689), on Sir Robert Filmer; as printed in Project Gutenberg ebook 7370
suggested_refs: The 1690-dated first edition of the Two Treatises, and Locke's hand-corrected copies

stops.name: Oates, the room in the Essex house
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1691; no month. Coordinates standardised: the research lenses carried four different pairs for this one parish, from 51.75/0.2333 to 51.7717/0.217. The manor house was demolished and its footprint is approximate in any case.
stops.campa: He takes rooms at Oates, the Masham house in the Essex parish of High Laver, twenty miles northeast of London, and never lives anywhere else again. Damaris Masham runs the household and writes philosophy inside it. Locke pays board, keeps his library in an upper room, teaches the Masham boy, and rides to London when the Board of Trade requires him there. His lungs cannot manage London coal. The manor is pulled down long afterward, and its exact footprint has to be taken from parish maps.
suggested_refs: The site of Oates Manor, High Laver, and the parish maps that fix it

stops.name: London, the two anonymous books of the nineties
stops.date_confidence: attested: Some Thoughts Concerning Education 1693, The Reasonableness of Christianity 1695, the second anonymous. Months not given.
stops.campa: Some Thoughts Concerning Education appears in 1693, assembled out of letters he had written to a friend about bringing up a son: fresh air, cold feet, no beating, no rote, a mind furnished rather than filled. The Reasonableness of Christianity follows in 1695, anonymously, and is at once accused of Socinianism, of shrinking the creed to a single article a man might reach by thinking. Busby's birch and the catechism of Westminster are both being answered, forty-six years late, by a man who will not sign his name to the answer.
suggested_refs: The 1693 first edition of Some Thoughts Concerning Education, and the Socinianism controversy of 1695-97

stops.name: Trinity College, the letter of the sixteenth of September
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the letter is dated and quoted directly in newton.journey.json. Pin inherited byte-identical from that file.
stops.campa: Isaac Newton, in the worst months of his life, writes to Locke by name on the sixteenth of September, accusing him of endeavouring to embroil him with woemen and asking his pardon for having thought ill of him. The two have corresponded for years, Fellows of the same Society, arguing over chemistry and over the interpretation of scripture. Locke answers gently and keeps the letter. Newton recovers within the year and never explains it. A century later a poet will name these two men together as a single enemy.
suggested_refs: The Newton-Locke correspondence of 1690-1704, including the letter of 16 September 1693

stops.name: Whitehall, the Commissioner of Trade
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1696-1700; he is described as an active commissioner throughout, taking periodic lodgings in Westminster to attend sessions.
stops.campa: He is made a Commissioner of the Board of Trade and becomes its most industrious member, shaping English colonial and economic policy at close range: the coinage, the colonies and their governors, the terms of trade. He takes lodgings near Whitehall to attend the sessions and dislikes the smoke of the place. The reports go out over the Board's name and not over his. The Second Treatise is on the shelves of the same city, in its second edition and still unsigned, and nobody at the Board connects the two.
stops.quote: freedom of men under government is, to have a standing rule to live by, common to every one of that society
stops.quote_source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), Chapter IV, Section 22; Project Gutenberg ebook 7370
suggested_refs: The minute books of the Board of Trade and Plantations, 1696-1700

stops.name: Oates, the commission given up
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1700 with worsening asthma given as the reason; the month is not recorded and June is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He gives up the commission in 1700, his asthma no longer letting him breathe London air well enough to do the work, and withdraws to Oates for good. He is sixty-eight. From there he answers correspondence and keeps at the text of the Essay, which has never satisfied him: he corrects a third edition by hand and leaves a fourth in the care of friends. About the Two Treatises he says nothing publicly at all. The manuscript is more than half lost and the printed text is still wrong.
suggested_refs: Locke's hand-corrected copies of the Essay and the Two Treatises, prepared 1698-1704

stops.name: Oates, the reading of the Psalms
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The pool's claim that he never acknowledged the Two Treatises in his lifetime is corrected: he named the work in a codicil to his will, signed weeks before his death, which became public only when the will was read.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of October, in his rooms at Oates, Damaris Masham reads the Psalms aloud to him and he dies while she is reading. He is seventy-two, in the house of the woman he met in London twenty-two years before. Weeks earlier he had signed a codicil to his will naming himself as the author of Two Treatises of Government. Fifteen years he let the book stand unsigned, through two revolutions in its reputation, and the acknowledgement becomes public only when the will is opened and read out.
suggested_refs: The codicil to Locke's will, 1704, acknowledging the authorship of the Two Treatises

stops.name: All Saints, High Laver: the brick tomb outside the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1704; the day is not recorded. The epitaph is his own composition, with friends adding only the two dates.
stops.campa: They bury him in the churchyard of All Saints, High Laver, outside the south wall of the nave and under a brick altar tomb, not inside the church. The Latin on the marble is his own. He wrote it before he died and left his friends only the dates to fill in. It tells the traveller who stops that here lies a man content with his own small fortune, bred a scholar, who made his learning subservient only to truth, and it directs anyone who wants his character to look for it in his writings instead.
stops.quote: Siste Viator, Hic juxta situs est JOHANNES LOCKE
stops.quote_source: Locke's self-composed Latin epitaph, All Saints' Church, High Laver, Essex, 1704
suggested_refs: The brick altar tomb of John Locke, south of the nave of All Saints, High Laver

segments.name: The Afterlife of an Abridged Book

stops.name: Amsterdam, the French Locke with its first hundred pages gone
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1691 for Mazel's French translation and for its omissions; the source gives only 'in the Netherlands' and names no city, so the pin is the canonical Amsterdam pin standing in for an unspecified Dutch imprint.
stops.campa: A Huguenot exile named David Mazel publishes a French Locke in the Netherlands two years after the English, and quietly drops the preface, the whole of the First Treatise, and the opening chapter of the Second. What is left begins at the state of nature and reads as a treatise on government in the abstract, with the demolition of Filmer gone out of it. Montesquieu, Voltaire, and Rousseau all meet Locke's politics in this truncated version. For a century the Continent argues with a book that is missing its first hundred pages.
stops.quote: Perhaps no man ever had a more judicious or more methodical genius, or was a more acute logician than Mr. Locke
stops.quote_source: Voltaire, Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733), Letter XIII, 'On Mr. Locke'; Project Gutenberg ebook 2445
suggested_refs: David Mazel's Du gouvernement civil (1691) and its silent omissions

stops.name: Chambery, a clerk reading without a teacher
stops.date_confidence: attested in jean_jacques_rousseau.journey.json for the Chambery land-registry years around 1731; pin inherited byte-identical from that file. The further claim that the Two Treatises is the acknowledged scaffold of Du contrat social is inference, not a statement in any file.
stops.campa: In the land registry at Chambery a young Savoyard clerk reads Locke alongside Descartes and Voltaire, with no teacher and in no order, taking what he can from each. Jean-Jacques Rousseau spends the rest of his life arguing with these books. Thirty-one years later Marc-Michel Rey prints Du contrat social at Amsterdam, the city where Locke had finished the Essay in hiding, and the argument that a people may unmake its own government comes back into the world in French, harder and hotter and much less English.
stops.quote: Such a multitude of reasoners having written the romance of the soul, a sage at last arose, who gave, with an air of the greatest modesty, the history of it.
stops.quote_source: Voltaire, Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733), Letter XIII, 'On Mr. Locke'; Project Gutenberg ebook 2445
sources: jean_jacques_rousseau.journey.json (stops 'Chambery: the land registry' and 'Amsterdam: Du contrat social off Rey's press')
suggested_refs: Rousseau's Confessions on the Chambery reading, and Rey's 1762 Amsterdam printing of Du contrat social

stops.name: Boston, the only American printing
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1773 as the sole eighteenth-century American edition, carrying the same omissions as Mazel's French; no month given.
stops.campa: Two Treatises of Government is printed at Boston in 1773, the only American edition of the century, and it carries the same holes as the French: no preface, no First Treatise, no opening chapter. The town that prints it throws tea into its own harbour in December. No further American edition follows for more than a hundred years. The republic that cites the book most often is reading it, through that whole century, in an abridgement and at second hand.
stops.quote: Whatsoever then he removes out of the state that nature hath provided, and left it in, he hath mixed his labour with, and joined to it something that is his own, and thereby makes it his property.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), Chapter V, Section 27; Project Gutenberg ebook 7370
suggested_refs: The 1773 Boston edition of the Two Treatises and its collation against the London text

stops.name: Independence Hall, the self-evident truths
stops.date_confidence: the adoption is attested and the pin is inherited byte-identical from thomas_jefferson.journey.json. The Lockean descent is inference: that file does not name Locke at this stop. Jefferson's separate ranking of Locke with Bacon and Newton is attested from his correspondence.
stops.campa: In the Pennsylvania State House a draft is adopted holding certain truths to be self-evident: that all men are created equal, and endowed with unalienable rights, among these life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Locke's triad had been life, liberty, and estate. The document does not name him, and the substitution has been argued over ever since. Thomas Jefferson later ranks Locke with Bacon and Newton as the three greatest men who ever lived, for laying the foundations of physical and moral science.
stops.quote: TO understand political power right, and derive it from its original, we must consider, what state all men are naturally in, and that is, a state of perfect freedom to order their actions, and dispose of their possessions and persons, as they think fit, within the bounds of the law of nature, without asking leave, or depending upon the will of any other man.
stops.quote_source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), Chapter II, Section 4; Project Gutenberg ebook 7370
sources: Wikipedia, 'Two Treatises of Government', citing Jefferson's correspondence
suggested_refs: Jefferson's Rough Draught of the Declaration, and his letter ranking Bacon, Newton, and Locke

stops.name: Felpham, the letter against single vision
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the letter is dated and quoted directly in william_blake.journey.json. Pin inherited byte-identical from that file.
stops.campa: From a cottage on the Sussex coast William Blake writes on the twenty-second of November that he sees fourfold, and names what he is set against: single vision, and Newton's sleep. Locke stands beside Newton in that indictment throughout Blake's work, the two of them welded into one enemy, the mind that measures and the mind that doubts. Ninety-eight years after his death the modest man who asked to be looked for in his writings is being read as a demon of reason by a poet who has read him closely.
sources: william_blake.journey.json (stop 'Felpham, the letter of the fourfold vision')
suggested_refs: Blake's letter from Felpham of 22 November 1802, on fourfold vision and Newton's sleep

stops.name: All Saints, High Laver: the tablet taken indoors
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1932; no month recorded.
stops.campa: In 1932 the marble tablet carrying the epitaph is lifted off the outer wall and set up inside the church, to save the lettering from Essex weather. The brick tomb stays where it is, in the grass by the south nave wall, and the words he wrote for a passing traveller to stop and read are now behind a door that is usually locked. At Wrington, at the other end of England, his bust stands in the church porch beside Hannah More. The body lies in one place and the sentence he composed for it in another.
suggested_refs: The mural tablet of John Locke, moved inside All Saints, High Laver, in 1932
